wellness.title: Swiss Primary Care Trial Adds to Clinical Evidence for Pelargonium Sidoides Extract
wellness.teaser: A 2026 randomised controlled trial in Swiss primary care compared Pelargonium sidoides extract against usual care for acute bronchitis, adding to a substantial existing body of clinical research.
wellness.body:
Published in a Nature Portfolio respiratory care journal in 2026, the PHYTOBRONCH trial, led by Bourqui, Corpataux, Bonofiglio and colleagues, tested EPs 7630, the standardised Pelargonium sidoides extract marketed as Umckaloabo or Kaloba, against usual care for acute bronchitis in a pragmatic, open-label, randomised design conducted across Swiss primary care practices. Pragmatic trial designs are specifically built to reflect how a treatment performs in ordinary clinical practice rather than under the tightly controlled conditions of an explanatory trial, which makes this a particularly relevant test of the extract's real-world usefulness.

This trial adds to an already substantial body of clinical research on Pelargonium sidoides extract. A 2026 review in Phytochemistry Letters, by Khameli, Lewu, Mulaudzi and Adebo, examined the plant's phytochemical complexity and pharmacological significance more broadly, noting findings on the extract's effect on the replication of various respiratory viruses, alongside reference to a separate open-label randomised clinical trial. Extracts derived from a single South African plant species being tested in Swiss primary care, and reviewed in international phytochemistry literature, within the same year, reflects a genuinely unusual level of sustained clinical attention for an African medicinal plant.

This information is provided for educational purposes and does not constitute medical advice. Anyone experiencing bronchitis or another respiratory condition should consult a qualified healthcare professional before using Pelargonium sidoides or any extract derived from it.
source_urls: Bourqui, A., Corpataux, O., Bonofiglio, F. et al., "Pelargonium sidoides extract (EPs 7630) versus usual care for acute bronchitis in Swiss primary care (PHYTOBRONCH): a pragmatic, open-label, randomised controlled trial," NPJ Primary Care Respiratory Medicine, 2026
Khameli, K., Lewu, M.N., Mulaudzi, T., Adebo, O.A. et al., "Phytochemical complexity, pharmacological significance and developed products of Pelargonium sidoides DC," Phytochemistry Letters, 2026

innovation.title: Antiviral Activity Against Respiratory Viruses Broadens Pelargonium Sidoides Research
innovation.teaser: Recent phytochemical review work highlights Pelargonium sidoides extract's effect on respiratory virus replication, extending its research profile beyond its established antibacterial reputation.
innovation.body:
Most of Pelargonium sidoides's clinical reputation has been built on bacterial respiratory infections, bronchitis in particular, supported by decades of research behind the EPs 7630 extract sold as Umckaloabo and Kaloba. A 2026 review in Phytochemistry Letters, by Khameli and colleagues, draws attention to a different and comparatively newer line of investigation: the extract's effect on the replication of various respiratory viruses, a mechanism distinct from its antibacterial action.

This distinction matters practically. A treatment effective against both bacterial and viral respiratory pathogens would have considerably broader clinical utility than one limited to bacterial infections, particularly given how difficult it can be, in ordinary clinical practice, to distinguish quickly between viral and bacterial causes of a respiratory illness. The review does not claim this dual action is fully established or clinically proven at the same evidentiary level as the extract's antibacterial effects, which have decades of trial data behind them, but it does mark a genuine expansion of the research questions being asked about this single plant extract.

The commercial infrastructure already built around EPs 7630, an established, patented, internationally distributed product, means that any confirmed antiviral activity would likely translate into product development considerably faster than it would for a compound without existing manufacturing and regulatory pathways already in place.
source_urls: Khameli, K., Lewu, M.N., Mulaudzi, T., Adebo, O.A. et al., "Phytochemical complexity, pharmacological significance and developed products of Pelargonium sidoides DC," Phytochemistry Letters, 2026

ik.title: Xhosa and Sotho Names Reflect Deep Traditional Use of Pelargonium Sidoides
ik.teaser: Known as ikubalo and iyeza lesikhali in Xhosa, Pelargonium sidoides carries a traditional medicinal identity that predates its European commercial name by generations.
ik.body:
SANBI's own record gives the Xhosa names for Pelargonium sidoides as ikubalo and iyeza lesikhali, alongside khoara-e-nyenyane in Southern Sotho, names reflecting generations of use by these communities long before the plant's German commercial name, Umckaloabo, entered international trade. This naming detail matters beyond simple linguistic interest. It corrects a common misattribution, since umckaloabo is frequently, and incorrectly, presented as an indigenous South African name when it is in fact the German trade name given to the commercial extract product.

The actual Xhosa and Sotho names point to traditional use practices that predate any German pharmaceutical involvement by a considerable margin, use that centred on respiratory and gastrointestinal complaints long before European researchers identified the plant's antibacterial properties in a laboratory setting. This pattern, a plant's genuine indigenous name being displaced in popular understanding by a later commercial or trade name, is not unique to Pelargonium sidoides, but it is worth correcting specifically here given how widely the umckaloabo name has spread internationally.

Recognising the correct Xhosa and Sotho names is a small but meaningful step toward ensuring the communities whose traditional knowledge underpins this now-globally distributed medicine are properly credited, rather than having their contribution obscured behind a foreign trade name.

people.title: Eastern Cape Harvesters Face Real Pressure from Pelargonium Sidoides's Global Success
people.teaser: Historical research recorded over 26 tonnes of Pelargonium sidoides harvested in a single month across nine Eastern Cape villages, reflecting both the plant's commercial value and the strain that value places on wild populations.
people.body:
Research by Lewu, published in 2007 and cited 66 times since, documented an estimated 26.3 tonnes of Pelargonium sidoides harvested within a single month across nine villages in the Eastern Cape, at a time when the plant's export-driven harvest rate had increased substantially alongside rising international demand, with the broader industry value estimated at around 150 million US dollars annually. These figures, though now nearly two decades old, established the scale of commercial pressure this plant has been under for a considerable period, pressure that predates and likely exceeds what most other South African medicinal plants have experienced.

The villages and harvesters behind these figures are not incidental to Pelargonium sidoides's global commercial success. They are the people whose labour and traditional harvesting knowledge directly supplied the raw material behind a pharmaceutical product now distributed across Europe and beyond under the Umckaloabo and Kaloba names. Whether the economic benefit flowing from that international success has reached these specific Eastern Cape communities proportionately to the value they generate remains a question the historical research on benefit-sharing, discussed elsewhere in this profile, suggests has not been fully or satisfactorily resolved.

The government's more recent revision of the species' Biodiversity Management Plan, dated February 2026, specifically aims to ensure all sub-populations of Pelargonium sidoides continue to persist in nature, a regulatory response that implicitly acknowledges the kind of harvest pressure Lewu's earlier research documented has not disappeared over the intervening years.
source_urls: Lewu, F.B., "Commercial harvesting of Pelargonium sidoides in the Eastern Cape," 2007

agronomy.title: Revised Government Management Plan Targets Long-Term Survival of Wild Pelargonium Sidoides
agronomy.teaser: A February 2026 revision of the species' Biodiversity Management Plan specifically aims to keep all sub-populations of Pelargonium sidoides persisting in the wild.
agronomy.body:
The Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment published a revised Biodiversity Management Plan for Pelargonium sidoides in February 2026, running to 68 pages and stating its aim explicitly: ensuring that all sub-populations of the species continue to persist in nature. A Biodiversity Management Plan of this kind is a formal regulatory instrument under South African environmental law, typically triggered when a species faces documented population pressure serious enough to warrant a coordinated, government-level conservation response rather than informal or purely voluntary industry measures.

This level of formal regulatory attention reflects the sustained harvest pressure documented over nearly two decades, from Lewu's 2007 research recording tens of tonnes harvested monthly across a handful of Eastern Cape villages, through to the present day. A species surviving under this kind of pressure for this long, while still supporting an ongoing international pharmaceutical supply chain, suggests either that wild populations have proven more resilient than initially feared, or that the pressure has simply not yet reached a tipping point, a distinction the revised management plan's specific measures should help clarify as they are implemented.

The plan's focus on sub-populations, rather than the species as a single national population, suggests a geographically nuanced management approach, recognising that harvest pressure and population health likely vary considerably across the plant's different growing areas within the Eastern Cape rather than being uniform.
source_urls: Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, Government Gazette, Biodiversity Management Plan, 27 February 2026

legislation.title: African Centre for Biosafety's Patent Challenge Remains a Landmark Case for Pelargonium Sidoides
legislation.teaser: The 2008 patent challenge against Schwabe's Umckaloabo extraction process, brought by the African Centre for Biosafety, remains one of the clearest examples of benefit-sharing disputes involving South African indigenous plants.
legislation.body:
In 2008, the African Centre for Biosafety, a South African non-governmental organisation, formally challenged a European patent held by Schwabe covering the extraction process used to produce Umckaloabo, the commercial Pelargonium sidoides extract, citing concerns over the appropriation of Xhosa and Sotho traditional knowledge without adequate recognition or benefit-sharing. Academic research by van Niekerk and Wynberg, published in Development Southern Africa in 2012 and cited 43 times, documents this challenge and its broader implications for how South Africa's indigenous plants are commercialised internationally.

This case predates, and in some respects anticipates, the more structured benefit-sharing frameworks later established for plants such as rooibos and hoodia. It remains relevant today precisely because the underlying tension it raised, whether a European pharmaceutical patent covering an extraction process adequately recognises the South African traditional knowledge that identified the plant's properties in the first place, has not been definitively resolved as a general principle, even where specific cases have reached individual settlements or outcomes.

Given the scale of harvest activity documented in the Eastern Cape and the substantial ongoing commercial value of Umckaloabo internationally, this patent challenge deserves continued attention as a reference case for how future indigenous-plant commercialisation disputes in South Africa might be approached, rather than being treated as a closed historical episode.
source_urls: van Niekerk, J., Wynberg, R., "The trade in Pelargonium sidoides: Rural livelihood relief or bounty for the 'bio-buccaneers'?," Development Southern Africa, 2012

projects.title: Government Biodiversity Plan Marks a Renewed Conservation Push for Pelargonium Sidoides
projects.teaser: The February 2026 revision of the national Biodiversity Management Plan represents a concrete, current government initiative to secure the species' long-term wild survival.
projects.body:
The Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment's revised Biodiversity Management Plan for Pelargonium sidoides, published in the Government Gazette in February 2026, represents active, current government engagement with a conservation challenge that has been documented for close to two decades. Running to 68 pages, the plan's explicit goal is ensuring all sub-populations of the species continue to persist in nature, language that suggests a detailed, population-by-population approach rather than a single blanket national policy.

Projects of this scale and formality typically involve substantial input from conservation scientists, harvester communities, and industry stakeholders during their drafting, though the specific consultation process behind this particular revision is not detailed in what is publicly summarised. What is clear is that a species supporting a well-established international pharmaceutical product, with documented harvest volumes in the tens of tonnes monthly from historical research, has reached a point where the government considers a formal, updated management response necessary.

The practical test of this plan's effectiveness will only become visible over the coming years, as population monitoring data either confirms stabilisation of wild sub-populations or reveals the plan requires further strengthening, making this a genuinely live, ongoing initiative worth revisiting as new information becomes available rather than a finished undertaking.
source_urls: Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, Government Gazette, Biodiversity Management Plan, 27 February 2026

intelligence.title: Established Clinical Pipeline and Tightening Conservation Rules Shape Pelargonium Sidoides's Outlook
intelligence.teaser: Continued clinical trial activity supports Pelargonium sidoides's established pharmaceutical position, while a renewed government conservation plan signals tighter future harvest oversight.
intelligence.body:
Pelargonium sidoides occupies an unusual position among South African medicinal plants covered in this registry: it already underpins a mature, internationally distributed pharmaceutical product, Umckaloabo and Kaloba, built on the EPs 7630 extract, with continued clinical trial activity as recent as 2026 in Swiss primary care. This is a considerably more advanced commercial and clinical stage than most indigenous South African plants have reached, and it means the near-term intelligence picture centres less on whether commercial viability exists, since it clearly already does, and more on supply security and regulatory direction.

The February 2026 revision of the species' Biodiversity Management Plan is the development most likely to affect future supply. Historical harvest data documented tens of tonnes monthly from a small number of Eastern Cape villages, a rate that has evidently sustained the export pharmaceutical supply chain for close to two decades but has also prompted renewed formal government intervention. Any tightening of harvest quotas or permit conditions arising from this plan's implementation could meaningfully affect raw material availability for the existing pharmaceutical supply chain.

For commercial entities with an existing or prospective interest in Pelargonium sidoides, the combination of an established, clinically validated product with genuine, formally documented conservation constraints on its raw material supply represents a distinctive risk profile, mature market demand paired with tightening upstream supply conditions, worth factoring into any sourcing or investment decision. This is market observation, not investment advice, and any commercial decision should involve independent financial and legal guidance given the species' regulated conservation status.
source_urls: Bourqui, A. et al., NPJ Primary Care Respiratory Medicine, 2026
Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, Government Gazette, February 2026
